clinicalPearls: An inducible urticaria triggered by a rise in core body temperature, as with exercise, a hot bath or shower, emotional stress or eating spicy food
The eruption is highly distinctive, consisting of numerous small (1 to 3 mm) punctate weals surrounded by large erythematous flares
It is common in adolescents and young adults and is frequently accompanied by itching, pricking or burning
Provocation by exercise to the point of sweating, or by passive warming such as a hot shower or immersion in a warm bath, can reproduce the lesions and confirm the diagnosis
Severe episodes may occasionally be associated with systemic symptoms such as wheeze, abdominal cramps or faintness
It should be distinguished from exercise-induced anaphylaxis and from cold or solar urticaria triggered in similar situations
Management combines avoidance of abrupt overheating with non-sedating antihistamines, and omalizumab is an option for chronic, antihistamine-resistant disease
reference.pathophysiology: Cholinergic urticaria is triggered by an increase in core body temperature, in which cholinergic (acetylcholine-mediated) stimulation of eccrine sweat glands is linked to mast cell activation and histamine release, producing the characteristic small weals with surrounding flares. Proposed mechanisms include sensitivity to a component of sweat and impaired delivery or leakage of sweat, and in some patients a degree of sweat-related autoreactivity is demonstrable. The net effect is that any stimulus raising body temperature can provoke widespread mediator release in predisposed individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Solar urticaria when heat and sun exposure coincide
additionalInvestigations: Provocation by exercise or passive warming to reproduce the characteristic punctate weals
History linking episodes to exertion, heat, hot showers, emotion or spicy food
Assessment to distinguish it from exercise-induced anaphylaxis, including any food-dependent pattern
Consideration of an intradermal test with a cholinergic agent in specialist practice
Basic screening for chronic urticaria where features overlap
Evaluation for systemic symptoms in those reporting wheeze or faintness
redFlags: Wheeze, throat tightness, collapse or other features suggesting anaphylaxis
Symptoms strongly linked to exercise with food, raising concern for food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis
Frequent disabling attacks interfering with exercise or daily activity
reference.prognosis: Cholinergic urticaria often persists for several years but tends to improve over time, and most patients are well controlled with trigger moderation and antihistamines; the main concern is the small subset with associated systemic reactions, in whom careful assessment and an emergency plan may be needed.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for exercise-induced anaphylaxis, which has different implications and management
Advising complete avoidance of exercise rather than gradual acclimatisation and pre-treatment
Overlooking the diagnosis because the tiny weals are less familiar than large urticarial lesions
Failing to consider omalizumab or up-dosed antihistamines in resistant cases
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on chronic urticaria
management: First-line treatment is a second-generation non-sedating H1 antihistamine, up-titrated as needed for control
Advise moderation of triggers that raise core temperature, such as vigorous exercise, hot baths, emotional stress and spicy food
For refractory disease, consider add-on options such as an anticholinergic, propranolol, ketotifen or omalizumab
Consider graded heat exposure or sweat desensitisation to raise the provocation threshold
Provide an adrenaline auto-injector and a written emergency plan for the subset with systemic reactions such as wheeze or faintness
Distinguish and manage separately from exercise-induced anaphylaxis, referring to dermatology or allergy where the diagnosis is unclear
